A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Transolver-3 work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and sufficiently complete. Relocated pseudocode and renumbered appendix material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original Transolver-3 prediction results, aerodynamic coefficient predictions, memory and latency measurements, resolution analyses, and appendix visualizations, although some baseline results are attributed to earlier work.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds training-subset experiments, AirCraft results, a practical cost comparison, and repeated-run statistics.

M1.justification: The faster slice/deslice operations, geometry slice tiling, amortized training, and cached-state inference remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 moves from Appendix A.1 into the main text. Uniform sampling and FP32 accumulation are newly specified implementation details; FP64 and weighted Welford accumulation are suggested alternatives, not adopted components.

E1.justification: v2 retains NASA-CRM, AhmedML, and DrivAerML and adds the AirCraft dataset, described as containing transonic and supersonic flows with shocks and discontinuities (Section 4.2, Table 7). This extends aerodynamic evaluation coverage without introducing a different task family.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds MeshGraphNet across all three retained benchmarks, expanding the actual comparator set from seven to eight without removing existing baselines. AB-UPT also participates in the new direct training/inference cost comparison in Table 8.

E3.justification: The configuration table changes training subsets for AhmedML and DrivAerML from 400K cells in v1 Table 6 to 100K in v2 Table 9, a substantial reported setting revision that does not establish experiments were rerun. Added protocols include a 1K–100K training-subset sweep, training AirCraft with 100K of approximately 300K points, and an end-to-end cost comparison on one A100. Existing benchmark splits and accuracy metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained tiling, inference-resolution, and case-study analyses, v2 adds training-subset sensitivity tests, targeted evaluation on flows with shocks, and practical training/inference cost analysis (Tables 6–8). These substantially extend the evidence about amortized-training robustness and practical scalability.

E5.justification: v1 supplies no repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 Appendix B newly reports three repetitions and standard deviations for Transolver-3 across all ten main benchmark metrics in Table 10. This adds uncertainty reporting across the principal results, but provides no seeds, baseline uncertainties, or formal significance tests; it does not establish an increase over v1's actual run count.

E6.justification: Existing Table 4 scores remain unchanged, while v2 adds MeshGraphNet scores, subset-size results, AirCraft results, and resource measurements. Table 7 reports AirCraft errors of 5.80% for Transolver-3, 6.40% for Transolver++, and 6.93% for AB-UPT. Table 8 reports 36 versus 40 GPU hours but 260 versus 220 seconds inference latency for Transolver-3 versus AB-UPT. New Table 10 lists NASA-CRM pressure error as 8.72% with standard deviation 0.03%, while Table 4 still lists 8.71%.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects Equation (1) from W_Linear1 x to x W_Linear1, making multiplication consistent with the declared N-by-C feature matrix. The illustrative size relation also changes from C >= M to C approximately M. The complexity derivations and Remark 3.1's quadrature bound remain unchanged; no new proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same architectural contributions, scalability beyond 160 million cells, and performance claims on three main benchmarks. The added GeoPT discussion describes future work rather than a newly achieved contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new experiments as robustness to sparse training subsets and shocks, and discusses efficiency trade-offs against AB-UPT. Appendix A.4 adds numerical-stability reasoning, while Appendix D explicitly identifies untested generalization to transient and tightly coupled multiphysics systems. The tiling computation-memory trade-off was already discussed in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, specifies uniform sampling without replacement and FP32 accumulation, and documents A100 resource measurements. It also revises the reported training-subset sizes. The pseudocode is retained, although the earlier note about encapsulating checkpoint operations into one function is omitted.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citation of MeshGraphNet, cites weighted Welford statistics for possible numerical stabilization, and positions GeoPT as a future geometric-pretraining extension. The broader relationship to Transolver, Transolver++, and AB-UPT remains unchanged. Numerous other bibliography edits only abbreviate publication information.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 moves Algorithm 1 into Section 3.2, reorganizes appendix subsections around new stability, statistics, and limitations material, and adds targeted explanatory paragraphs. It also adds acknowledgements and replaces the preprint footer with conference publication information.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 6–8 and 10, expands Table 4 with a MeshGraphNet row, and relocates Algorithm 1 into a single-column main-text display. Existing Figures 1–15 retain their content, with several floats repositioned. The overall visual design remains intact.

improvement.justification: Tables 6–8 and 10 strengthen validation through training-subset sensitivity, shock-containing flows, practical resource trade-offs, and repeated-run variability. Added sampling details and explicit applicability limits improve transparency. These benefits are qualified by the unexplained 400K-to-100K configuration revision despite unchanged main scores, and by missing baseline uncertainty and formal tests supporting the new significance language.
